extractions.quote:
Case report
A healthy man aged 33 years had a tick bite in the left lower quadrant of the abdomen with no erythema 9 weeks before admission to our hospital.
Three months later, the patient had no further difficulty in walking.
From the 3rd week following the tick bite he experienced gradually increasing stiffness of the left calf and later also the thigh.
Clinically, his disease may be characterized as a partial stift man syndrome with muscle rigidity and painful myoclonic jerks confined to the left lower leg.

The week prior to admission he developed severe painful cramps of the leg muscles which occurred spontaneously and could be elicited by loud noises.

extractions.quote: The clinical picture of this patient showed some resemblance to the stift man syndrome. However, it was confined to one leg and its infectious origin was confirmed by CSF findings, positive serology and the demonstration of intrathecally produced, oligoclonal, B. burgdorferi-specific IgG bands.
Clinically, his disease may be characterized as a partial stift man syndrome with muscle rigidity and painful myoclonic jerks confined to the left lower leg.

Electromyographic analysis
Several electromygraphic (EMG) examinations revealed a tonic firing of normal motor units in the left leg muslces which could not be suppressed voluntarily, but no denervation activity or fasciculations.

Therapeutic trials with antispastic drugs showed moderate amelioration of cramps and ability to walk with tizanidine 3×6mg/day and baclofen 3x5mglday, but diazepam 3 x 5 mg/day was much more effective.
A magnetic resonance scan showed no abnormalities of brain or spinal cord either with or without gadolinium enhancement.
Local tetanus was initially considered, but unlikely with normal silent periods in the affected leg.
Lumbar puncture disclosed elevated cell counts and protein values (see Table 1) in the CSF.
The raised quotients for albumin and IgG indicated both a disruption of the blood-brain barrier and intrathecal synthesis of IgG at the first lumbar puncture.

No abnormalities of the deep tendon reflexes were seen except for an exaggerated ankle jerk on both sides and spontaneous as well as reflex myoclonus (induced, for example, by loud noise, touching or spraying the skin, taps to the leg tendons or even the bed) in his left leg.
A magnetic resonance scan showed no abnormalities of brain or spinal cord either with or without gadolinium enhancement.

During the following days the patient slowly improved. The jerks were not as severe as before treatment and could then onty be elicited by touching the affected leg or by a jolt to the bed, but no more by toud noise. However, walking was still markedly impaired. Eight weeks after the onset of symptoms, the patient was still not able to walk distances greater than a few hundred metres without muscle cramps in the left leg. Three months later, the patient had no further difficulty in walking.

Therapeutic trials with antispastic drugs showed moderate amelioration of cramps and ability to walk with tizanidine 3×6mg/day and baclofen 3x5mglday, but diazepam 3 x 5 mg/day was much more effective.

Therapy with 20 × 106 units/day penicillin G i.v. for 14 days was initiated. The patient also received 500 units of polyvalent human anti-tetanus antibodies i.m. (Behringwerke, Marburg, FRG) although localized tetanus was improbable because of the electrophysiological findings (see below).
